title: CSP: Failure to Define Directive with No Fallback
description: The Content Security Policy (CSP) fails to define one of the directives that does not fall back to default-src. Certain CSP directives—specifically frame-ancestors, form-action, base-uri, and sandbox—do not inherit values from the generic default-src directive. Omitting them from the CSP definition allows the browser to default to permitting any origin/behavior for that feature, potentially leaving the application vulnerable to Clickjacking or UI redressing attacks.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send an HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/embed?zoom.
2. Inspect the Content-Security-Policy header in the HTTP response body.
3. Observe that specific non-fallback directives (such as frame-ancestors) are either missing, empty, or incorrectly defined.
proof_of_concept:
HTTP
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https: wss: blob: data:; img-src 'self' data: blob: https:; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self'; worker-src 'self' blob:; font-src 'self' data: https:; media-src 'self' data: blob: https:; frame-src 'none'; frame-ancestors '; base-uri 'self'; object-src 'none'; form-action 'none'

Verification Bash:
curl -I -s "https://www.worldmonitor.app/embed?zoom" | grep -i "content-security-policy"
business_impact: Directives like frame-ancestors govern which external sites can embed the application within an <iframe>, <frame>, <embed>, or <applet>. If frame-ancestors is omitted or malformed, attacker-controlled malicious websites can frame this application page and execute Clickjacking attacks, tricking authenticated users into making unintended UI actions.
remediation: Ensure all non-fallback CSP directives (frame-ancestors, form-action, base-uri) are explicitly and validly defined in the policy.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Ensure all non-fallback CSP directives (frame-ancestors, form-action, base-uri) are explicitly and validly defined in the policy.
2. To prevent the site from being framed by external sites (mitigating Clickjacking), set frame-ancestors to 'none' or 'self':
   Content-Security-Policy: ... frame-ancestors 'none';
3. Regularly audit CSP deployments using automated policy evaluators.

evidence.caption: PoC 1.1: Content-Security-Policy Alert & Header Inspection in ZAP
PoC 1.2: Response Header Inspection in OWASP ZAP (Missing Fallback)
PoC 1.3: Frame-ancestors Header Directive Verification in Browser DevTools

title: CSP: Wildcard Directive
description: Content Security Policy (CSP) is an added layer of security that helps to detect and mitigate certain types of attacks, including (but not limited to) Cross Site Scripting (XSS), and data injection attacks. These attacks are used for everything from data theft to site defacement or distribution of malware. CSP provides a set of standard HTTP headers that allow website owners to declare approved sources of content that browsers should be allowed to load on that page — covered types are JavaScript, CSS, HTML frames, fonts, images and embeddable objects such as Java applets, ActiveX, audio and video files.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send an HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/dashboard.
2. Inspect the HTTP response headers.
3. Observe the Content-Security-Policy header contains broad wildcard directives (such as https: under connect-src and img-src).
proof_of_concept:
HTTP Response Header Evidence:
default-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https: wss: blob: data: https://*.ingest.sentry.io ... (The policy contains wildcard source specifiers such as https:, wss:, and wildcard subdomains like https://*.vercel.app or https://*.dodopayments.com)
business_impact: Permissive wildcards (e.g., https: or wss:) allow the application to connect to or load assets from any arbitrary HTTPS endpoint on the internet, effectively bypassing origin restrictions and permitting exfiltration or injection if a secondary vulnerability exists.
remediation: Replace overly broad wildcard directives (such as https:, wss:, or wildcard subdomains) with explicit, trusted origin hostnames.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Scope connect-src, img-src, and frame-src to explicit, authorized domains rather than entire protocols like https:.
2. Avoid using wildcard subdomains (*.example.com) unless strictly required across multi-tenant architecture.
3. Implement CSP reporting endpoints (report-uri / report-to) to detect anomalous asset requests.

evidence.caption: PoC 2: Broad Wildcard Directives (https:, wss:) in Content-Security-Policy

title: CSP: script-src unsafe-inline (Systemic)
description: Content Security Policy (CSP) is an added layer of security that helps to detect and mitigate certain types of attacks, including Cross Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection attacks. The application's Content Security Policy uses 'unsafe-inline' within the script-src directive, allowing inline scripts to execute. This significantly weakens the CSP protection mechanism against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send an HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/docs/documentation.
2. Inspect the HTTP response headers returned by the server.
3. Locate the content-security-policy header.
4. Verify that the header allows 'unsafe-inline' execution.
business_impact: While a weak CSP is not an exploit on its own, specifying 'unsafe-inline' strips away the primary defense-in-depth layer designed to block cross-site scripting (XSS). If a parameter on the application becomes vulnerable to XSS, attackers can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the user's browser, leading to session hijacking, sensitive data theft, or unauthorized actions on behalf of authenticated users.
remediation: Remove 'unsafe-inline' from the script-src and worker-src directives and adopt cryptographically secure nonces or hashes.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Remove 'unsafe-inline' from the script-src and worker-src directives.
2. Refactor inline scripts into external .js files served from trusted origins.
3. If inline scripts are strictly required, implement cryptographically secure nonces (e.g., script-src 'nonce-rAnd0m123') or hashes (e.g., script-src 'sha256-...') for specific allowed scripts. Ensure configured servers and proxies strictly enforce valid CSP headers across all documentation routes.

evidence.caption: PoC 3: script-src unsafe-inline Policy Weakness Captured in OWASP ZAP

title: CSP: style-src unsafe-inline (Systemic)
description: Content Security Policy (CSP) is an added layer of security that helps to detect and mitigate certain types of attacks, including Cross Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection attacks. These attacks are used for everything from data theft to site defacement or distribution of malware. The application's Content Security Policy includes 'unsafe-inline' within the style-src directive, allowing arbitrary inline style sheets and inline style attributes to execute.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send an HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/dashboard.
2. Inspect the HTTP response headers returned by the web server.
3. Locate the content-security-policy header.
4. Verify that style-src contains the 'unsafe-inline' directive.
proof_of_concept:
HTTP Header Evidence:
content-security-policy: default-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https: wss: blob: data: https://*.ingest.sentry.io; img-src 'self' data: blob: https:; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; ...

Verification Check:
Browser permits inline CSS blocks such as <style>body { display: none; }</style> or inline attributes like <div style="background-image: url(...)"> without raising CSP block errors in the console.
business_impact: Allowing 'unsafe-inline' for CSS allows attackers (if an HTML injection point exists) to inject arbitrary CSS styles. This can be abused for UI redressing, web defacement, phishing overlays, or CSS-based data exfiltration (such as abusing background-image: url(...) or CSS keyframe animations to exfiltrate sensitive values or anti-CSRF tokens token-by-token).
remediation: Remove 'unsafe-inline' from the style-src directive and move styling to external stylesheets or nonce-protected tags.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Remove 'unsafe-inline' from the style-src directive.
2. Move all inline styles into external CSS files served from the same domain or trusted origins.
3. If dynamic inline styles are necessary, implement cryptographically secure nonces (e.g., style-src 'nonce-rAnd0m123') or hashes (e.g., style-src 'sha256-...').
4. Ensure the web server, application server, or load balancer is configured to serve the updated CSP header across all environment instances.

evidence.caption: PoC 4: style-src unsafe-inline Directive Allowing Injected Styles

title: Content Security Policy (CSP) Header Not Set
description: Content Security Policy (CSP) is an added layer of security that helps to detect and mitigate certain types of attacks, including Cross Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection attacks. These attacks are used for everything from data theft to site defacement or distribution of malware. CSP provides a set of standard HTTP headers that allow website owners to declare approved sources of content that browsers should be allowed to load on that page — covered types are JavaScript, CSS, HTML frames, fonts, images and embeddable objects such as Java applets, ActiveX, audio and video files.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send an HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection.
2. Inspect the HTTP response headers returned by the server.
3. Observe that no Content-Security-Policy header is present in the server's response.
proof_of_concept:
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Date: Tue, 08 Sep 2026 10:36:22 GMT
Content-Type: text/html
Connection: keep-alive
X-Frame-Options: DENY
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
Cache-Control: private, max-age=0, no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, post-check=0, pre-check=0
Expires: Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:01 GMT
Referrer-Policy: same-origin
(Notice: No Content-Security-Policy header returned)
business_impact: Without a Content Security Policy header defined on this route, the client browser lacks defense-in-depth restrictions against content injection. If an attacker identifies an XSS or HTML injection vulnerability on this endpoint, the browser will execute any injected scripts or load external malicious resources without restriction, potentially compromising user session data or leading to site defacement.
remediation: Configure the edge proxy or web server to enforce CSP on all routes including error pages and utility paths.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Configure the web server, application framework, or edge proxy (e.g., Cloudflare/reverse proxy) to include a robust Content-Security-Policy header for all HTTP responses, including 404 and edge-generated endpoints.
2. Ensure the policy defines strict fallback directives (such as default-src 'self') and restricts untrusted origins for scripts, styles, and framed content.

evidence.caption: PoC 5: Missing Content-Security-Policy Header on HTTP 404 Response

title: Cross-Domain Misconfiguration (Systemic)
description: Web browser data loading may be possible due to a Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) misconfiguration on the web server. The web server returns the Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * HTTP response header, which permits any arbitrary third-party domain to make cross-domain read requests and read responses via browser APIs (such as fetch or XMLHttpRequest).
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send an HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/robots.txt from a client or custom origin (e.g., using curl or browser dev tools with an Origin: https://evil.com header).
2. Inspect the returned HTTP response headers.
3. Observe that the response includes access-control-allow-origin: *.
proof_of_concept:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Tue, 08 Sep 2026 10:28:22 GMT
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Connection: keep-alive
access-control-allow-origin: *
Age: 7557
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate
content-disposition: inline; filename="robots.www.txt"

Browser Verification:
fetch('https://www.worldmonitor.app/robots.txt').then(res => res.text()).then(console.log);
business_impact: The CORS misconfiguration permits cross-domain read requests from arbitrary origins. On public resources like robots.txt, the immediate risk is low. However, if wildcard or overly permissive CORS policies are broadly applied across authenticated endpoints or sensitive internal APIs on the domain, attackers can craft malicious sites that extract private user data or perform authenticated cross-site data harvesting on behalf of logged-in victims.
remediation: Restrict Access-Control-Allow-Origin to an explicit allowlist of trusted domains rather than using a wildcard (*).
remediation_recommendations:
1. Ensure sensitive or user-specific data is not exposed without authentication and explicit access controls.
2. Restrict the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header to an explicit whitelist of trusted domain names rather than using a wildcard (*).
3. If public resources (like static files or public assets) require cross-origin access, maintain CORS headers strictly on those specific routes and remove wildcard headers from sensitive API routes so the browser enforces the Same-Origin Policy (SOP).

title: Sub Resource Integrity Attribute Missing (Systemic)
description: The integrity attribute is missing on a script or link tag served by an external server. The integrity tag prevents an attacker who has gained access to this server from injecting a malicious content.
owasp: A08:2021 - Software and Data Integrity Failures
alert_reference: Passive (90003 - Sub Resource Integrity Attribute Missing)
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send an HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/.
2. Inspect the HTML document body returned in the response.
3. Locate externally hosted <script> or <link> tags (e.g., https://abacus.worldmonitor.app/script.js).
4. Verify that the <script> tag lacks an integrity attribute containing a cryptographic hash.
proof_of_concept:
HTML Evidence:
<script async defer src="https://abacus.worldmonitor.app/script.js"
data-website-id="e8800335-c853-46a8-8497-c993ed2f68bc"
data-domains="worldmonitor.app,www.worldmonitor.app,happy.worldmonitor.app"
nonce="wm-static-bootstrap"></script>
(Notice: No integrity="sha384-..." attribute)
business_impact: Loading external scripts without Subresource Integrity (SRI) exposes the web application to supply-chain attacks. If the third-party server hosting script.js or its Content Delivery Network (CDN) is compromised, an attacker can modify the remote JavaScript file to execute malicious code within the context of all application users, leading to credential theft, DOM manipulation, or session hijacking.
remediation: Generate and attach cryptographic SRI hash attributes alongside crossorigin="anonymous" for all external scripts.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Generate a cryptographic hash (e.g., SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512) of the target external resource.
2. Add the integrity attribute alongside crossorigin="anonymous" to all external <script> and <link> elements. Example:
   <script async defer src="https://abacus.worldmonitor.app/script.js" integrity="sha384-..." crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

evidence.caption: PoC 7: Script Tag Lacking Subresource Integrity (SRI) Hash

title: Cross-Domain JavaScript Source File Inclusion (Systemic)
description: The page includes one or more script files from a third-party domain. Loading JavaScript files from third-party domains introduces trust dependencies on external systems that are not directly under the control of the primary application domain.
owasp: A08:2021 - Software and Data Integrity Failures
alert_reference: Passive (10017 - Cross-Domain JavaScript Source File Inclusion)
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send an HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/.
2. Inspect the HTML response body returned by the server.
3. Locate any <script> elements loading scripts from cross-domain origins (e.g., https://abacus.worldmonitor.app/script.js).
proof_of_concept:
HTML Evidence:
<script async defer src="https://abacus.worldmonitor.app/script.js"
data-website-id="e8800335-c853-46a8-8497-c993ed2f68bc"
data-domains="worldmonitor.app,www.worldmonitor.app,happy.worldmonitor.app"
nonce="wm-static-bootstrap"></script>

Verification: Host abacus.worldmonitor.app differs from primary domain www.worldmonitor.app.
business_impact: Including scripts from cross-domain sources creates a reliance on external server security. If the third-party domain hosting the script is compromised or hijacked, an attacker could manipulate the hosted script content to execute malicious code within the context of the primary application users, leading to cross-site scripting (XSS), data interception, or session theft.
remediation: Host critical scripts locally on the primary domain or apply Subresource Integrity controls.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Ensure JavaScript source files are loaded from trusted sources, and the sources cannot be controlled by end users of the application.
2. Host critical scripts locally on the same origin domain whenever feasible.
3. Implement Subresource Integrity (SRI) attributes (e.g., integrity="sha384-...") on any external scripts that must be included from external domains to ensure their integrity is validated before execution.

evidence.caption: PoC 8: Cross-Domain JavaScript Source File Inclusion from External CDN

title: Strict-Transport-Security Header Not Set (Systemic)
description: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is a web security policy mechanism whereby a web server declares that complying user agents (such as a web browser) are to interact with it using only secure HTTPS connections (i.e. HTTP layered over TLS/SSL). HSTS is an IETF standards track protocol and is specified in RFC 6797.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send an HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/docs/sitemap.xml.
2. Inspect the HTTP response headers returned by the server.
3. Verify that the response lacks the Strict-Transport-Security header.
proof_of_concept:
ZAP Response Inspection for https://www.worldmonitor.app/docs/sitemap.xml:
The response header section does not contain any Strict-Transport-Security entry.

Bash Verification:
curl -I -s https://www.worldmonitor.app/docs/sitemap.xml | grep -i "strict-transport-security"
(Returns empty string)
business_impact: Without an HSTS header, browsers accessing the site may initially connect over unencrypted HTTP before being redirected to HTTPS. This brief window allows network-level attackers (e.g., Man-in-the-Middle on public Wi-Fi) to perform SSL stripping attacks, intercept user communications, or downgrade secure traffic to unencrypted HTTP.
remediation: Enforce HTTP Strict Transport Security across all routes and subdomains with a long max-age.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Ensure that your web server, application server, or load balancer is configured to enforce Strict-Transport-Security across all routes and subdomains.
2. Add the Strict-Transport-Security header to all HTTPS responses with a long duration (max-age), including subdomains:
   Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload

evidence.caption: PoC 9: Missing Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) Header in ZAP

title: Timestamp Disclosure - Unix (Systemic)
description: A timestamp was disclosed by the application/web server - Unix. Standard 10-digit or 13-digit numbers embedded in HTTP headers, responses, or API documentation are often flagged as potential Unix timestamps.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send an HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/api-versioning.md.
2. Inspect the HTTP response headers and body content.
3. Observe the presence of a numeric string matching a Unix timestamp format (e.g., 1782864000).
proof_of_concept:
HTTP Response Evidence:
Deprecation: 1782864000

Epoch conversion:
1782864000 resolves to: 2026-07-01 05:30:00 UTC
business_impact: This finding is typically a low-severity or informational finding. Unix timestamps disclosed in HTTP response headers or public static documents (like deprecation schedules or release notes) generally do not expose sensitive internal system state or pose a security threat. However, in certain contexts, disclosing server time, database creation times, or token generation times could aid an attacker in timing-based attacks.
remediation: Review timestamp disclosures to ensure they only reflect public release schedules and not sensitive operational tokens.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Manually review the endpoint to confirm that the disclosed timestamp data is not sensitive and cannot be aggregated to disclose exploitable patterns.
2. If the timestamp represents public operational data (such as API deprecation dates), accept the risk as an intentional exposure or mark it as an accepted baseline in scanner policies.

evidence.caption: PoC 10: Unix Timestamp Disclosure Flagged in API Response / Markdown

title: Information Disclosure - Suspicious Comments (634)
description: The response appears to contain suspicious comments which may help an attacker. Developers frequently leave inline code comments during testing or staging that reveal technical implementation details, internal routes, or third-party service logic.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send an HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/dashboard.
2. Inspect the returned HTML response body.
3. Search for HTML comment blocks (<!-- ... -->).
4. Locate the comment describing script loading behavior: <!-- Umami Analytics loads from the SPA after first paint/idle... -->.
proof_of_concept:
HTML Comment Evidence in Dashboard source:
<!-- Umami Analytics loads from the SPA after first paint/idle (not the document head) so a slowdown abacus origin -->
business_impact: While this specific comment is informational, leaving comments in production code leaks insight into frontend architecture, script initialization routines, and external dependencies. Attackers utilize leftover comments during reconnaissance to map out internal components or locate sensitive TODOs, API keys, or backend endpoint references.
remediation: Implement automated comment stripping in the production CI/CD minification pipeline.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Implement automated build scripts or minifiers (e.g., Terser, HTMLMinifier) during CI/CD to strip all HTML, CSS, and JavaScript comments prior to production deployment.
2. Review remaining source files to ensure no sensitive notes, credentials, or internal URLs are exposed in raw client-side code.

title: Modern Web Application (Systemic)
description: The application appears to be a modern web application (Single Page Application / Single Page Interface). If you need to explore it automatically, then the AJAX Spider may well be more effective than the standard spider.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send an HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/dashboard.
2. Inspect the HTTP response body returned by the server.
3. Observe the presence of <noscript> tags, client-side bundle scripts, or DOM rendering hooks indicative of client-side JavaScript frameworks.
proof_of_concept:
HTML Response Source:
<noscript><link rel="stylesheet" crossorigin href="/assets/embed-url-C9JUULiG.css" nonce="wm-static-bootstrap"></noscript>

Dynamic DOM rendering confirms SPA framework execution.

It alerts penetration testers that static crawling tools may miss dynamically rendered routes and endpoints, requiring execution-capable crawlers (such as the ZAP AJAX Spider or headless browser automation) to map the full application surface.

title: Re-examine Cache-control Directives (Systemic)
description: The cache-control header has not been set properly or is missing, allowing the browser and intermediate proxy servers to cache content. While caching is intended for static assets like CSS, JavaScript, or image files, pages containing dynamic user data or authenticated content should be explicitly instructed not to cache to prevent sensitive data exposure.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send an HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/dashboard.
2. Inspect the HTTP response headers returned by the server.
3. Locate the Cache-Control header and verify its directives (e.g., public, max-age=0, must-revalidate).
proof_of_concept:
HTTP Response Headers:
cache-control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate

Bash Verification:
curl -I -s https://www.worldmonitor.app/dashboard | grep -i "cache-control"
business_impact: Allowing dynamic or user-specific pages (like /dashboard) to be marked as public or cached locally can expose personal user data. On shared computers, non-authenticated users could potentially navigate back using the browser history or retrieve cached sensitive pages directly from the browser/proxy storage.
remediation: Use no-cache, no-store directives on authenticated routes; use immutable caching only for static assets.
remediation_recommendations:
1. For dynamic, authenticated, or sensitive endpoints, update the HTTP response headers to instruct browsers and intermediate caches not to store sensitive pages:
   Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate
   Pragma: no-cache
   Expires: 0
2. For purely static, public assets (e.g., public CSS/JS/images), consider using caching directives with immutability:
   Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

evidence.caption: PoC 13: Permissive Cache-Control Directives on Authenticated Dashboard

title: Retrieved from Cache (Systemic)
description: The content was retrieved from a shared cache. If the response data is sensitive, personal, or user-specific, this may result in sensitive information being leaked. In some cases, this may even result in a user gaining complete control of the session of another user, depending on the configuration of the caching components in use in their environment. This is primarily an issue where caching servers such as "proxy" caches are configured on the local network (e.g., corporate or educational environments).
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send an HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/api/story.
2. Inspect the returned HTTP response headers.
3. Check for the presence of the Age header (e.g., Age: 0), indicating that the response passed through or was served by an HTTP/1.1 compliant caching proxy.
proof_of_concept:
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Date: Tue, 08 Sep 2026 10:28:35 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Age: 0
Cache-Control: private, no-store

Bash Check:
curl -I -s https://www.worldmonitor.app/api/story | grep -i "Age:"
business_impact: When an application routes through intermediary proxy caches, responses marked with an Age header indicate shared cache participation. If sensitive dynamic API data or authentication redirects are cached on upstream network proxies, other users sharing the same network proxy could receive cached responses containing another user's session state or sensitive payload.
remediation: Validate that API endpoints do not expose sensitive data to upstream caching proxies.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Validate that the response does not contain sensitive, personal, or user-specific information.
2. For sensitive or session-bound API endpoints, ensure the application sends non-cacheable directives to prevent intermediate storage:
   Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private
   Pragma: no-cache
   Expires: 0

evidence.caption: PoC 14: Retrieved from Shared Cache with Age Header Detection

title: User Agent Fuzzer (Active Scan)
description: The User Agent Fuzzer active scan rule checks for differences in application behavior based on modified or fuzzed User-Agent HTTP request headers (e.g., simulating mobile devices, legacy browsers, or search engine web crawlers). It compares HTTP response status codes and response body hashes against baseline requests to identify potential logic variations, legacy routing, or access control anomalies triggered by specific clients.
parameter: Header User-Agent: Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 8.0; Windows NT 5.1)
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Send a baseline HTTP GET request to https://www.worldmonitor.app/dashboard using a standard browser User-Agent.
2. Send a second HTTP GET request to the same URL, replacing the User-Agent header with legacy browser or crawler strings such as Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 8.0; Windows NT 5.1).
3. Compare the resulting HTTP response status codes and body structures.
proof_of_concept:
HTTP Response with Legacy User-Agent:
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Date: Tue, 08 Sep 2026 10:57:47 GMT
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Connection: keep-alive
Cache-Control: private, max-age=0, no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

Bash Test:
curl -i -H "User-Agent: Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 8.0; Windows NT 5.1)" https://www.worldmonitor.app/dashboard
business_impact: This finding is informational. The HTTP 403 Forbidden status indicates that Cloudflare or edge web application firewalls (WAF) actively block or filter legacy and unsecure client browser strings. No security bypass or unauthorized exposure was observed.
remediation: Document edge filtering rules and verify legitimate search crawlers are not inadvertently blocked.
remediation_recommendations:
1. No technical code fix is required if blocking obsolete user agents is an intended edge firewall or WAF security policy.
2. If specific legacy user agents or search engine crawlers require access, ensure WAF and routing rules explicitly permit them without exposing deprecated or insecure legacy site versions.

evidence.caption: PoC 15: User Agent Fuzzer Testing Yielding HTTP 403 WAF Filter Response

title: Wildcard postMessage / Missing Origin Validation
description: The application uses window.postMessage() with the target origin set to '*'. Data including storedHtml is sent without restricting delivery to a specific trusted origin. This may permit cross-origin message abuse if the receiving context is not strictly controlled.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Run the application in an authorized local testing environment.
2. Navigate to Live Webcams.
3. Inspect iframe communication.
4. Confirm the postMessage target origin is '*'.
5. Determine whether an unintended origin can receive the message.
business_impact: If the receiving context can be controlled or trusted incorrectly, information may be delivered to an unintended origin. Impact depends on the data transmitted and surrounding application logic.
remediation: Replace '*' with an explicit trusted origin allowlist. Validate event.origin on the receiving side and avoid sending sensitive data to untrusted contexts.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Replace '*' with an explicit trusted origin allowlist (e.g., 'https://app.worldmonitor.com').
2. Validate event.origin strictly on the receiving window message listener before processing payload data.
3. Avoid transmitting sensitive authentication state or rendered HTML markup over postMessage channels.

title: Insecure WebSocket Communication
description: Static analysis identified WebSocket communication using an insecure ws:// connection. Unencrypted WebSocket traffic may be exposed to interception or modification on an untrusted network.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Run the application locally.
2. Open the military-flight functionality.
3. Inspect browser network connections.
4. Check the WebSocket URL.
5. Determine whether it uses ws:// rather than wss://.
business_impact: Information transmitted through an unencrypted WebSocket may be observable or modifiable by a network attacker positioned on the communication path.
remediation: Use wss:// with properly configured TLS. Ensure certificates are validated and the server supports secure WebSocket connections.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Enforce wss:// exclusively for all WebSocket endpoints across all production and staging environments.
2. Verify TLS certificate validation is enabled and disallow fallback to plaintext ws:// connections.
3. Configure load balancers and reverse proxies to terminate TLS securely for WebSocket sessions.

title: Potential Path Traversal
description: Static analysis identified a potential path-traversal data flow. The risk exists if attacker-controlled input can influence a filesystem path and cause access outside an intended directory.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Run the application locally.
2. Identify the input influencing the filesystem path.
3. Determine whether it is user-controlled.
4. Use a harmless traversal value such as ../test.txt.
5. Verify whether path resolution remains within the intended directory.
proof_of_concept:
Safe Proof of Concept:
Create a local test directory containing an allowed file and a separate harmless test file outside it. Attempt to reference the outside test file using ../ and confirm that secure behavior denies access.
business_impact: If confirmed, path traversal could permit unauthorized access to files outside the application's intended directory.
remediation: Validate paths, use an allowlist, canonicalize paths, and verify the final resolved path remains inside the approved base directory.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Validate and canonicalize all file paths using path.resolve() or path.normalize().
2. Maintain an explicit allowlist of permitted map assets and configuration directories.
3. Reject any input containing traversal sequences such as '..' or null bytes.

title: Dynamic URL / Potential Arbitrary File Read
description: Static analysis identified dynamic URL handling in the Python SDK that may allow an attacker-controlled URL to reach a file or network retrieval operation. The complete source-to-sink flow must be verified.
parameter: Caller-controlled URL parameter in SDK client
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Run the SDK in an isolated local environment.
2. Identify the URL-accepting function.
3. Determine whether its URL is caller-controlled.
4. Supply a harmless URL hosted by a local test server.
5. Observe whether the SDK attempts retrieval.
proof_of_concept:
Safe Proof of Concept:
Use only a local HTTP server such as http://127.0.0.1:8000/test.txt and verify that the SDK attempts the request. Do not access cloud metadata, internal corporate systems, or third-party infrastructure.
business_impact: If arbitrary destinations are accepted, the application may access unintended local or remote resources.
remediation: Allowlist URL schemes and destinations, validate hosts, restrict outbound network access, and reject unexpected protocols or destinations.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Restrict URL schemes strictly to HTTPS.
2. Validate that destination hostnames belong to the official World Monitor API domains.
3. Disallow file://, gopher://, or internal IP addresses (e.g., 169.254.169.254, 127.0.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8).

title: Unsafe Object.assign() / Potential Mass Assignment
description: Static analysis identified Object.assign() involving application-controlled objects. This can become dangerous when client-controlled properties are copied into security-sensitive objects without an allowlist.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Run the local API server.
2. Identify request fields reaching Object.assign().
3. Determine whether those fields are client-controlled.
4. Submit a harmless unexpected property.
5. Check whether it is copied into the target object.
proof_of_concept:
Safe Proof of Concept:
Use a harmless property such as {"unexpectedField":"test"} and observe whether it is copied. Do not modify privileged or security-sensitive fields.
business_impact: If users can modify fields they should not control, mass assignment may allow unauthorized changes to application state or security-related properties.
remediation: Use explicit property allowlists or construct objects field-by-field. Do not blindly merge request objects into privileged objects.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Destructure only expected, safe fields from incoming request payloads.
2. Avoid Object.assign() or spread operators directly with unchecked user request bodies.
3. Apply schema validation libraries (such as Zod) to reject unexpected or unknown keys.

title: Unsanitized HTML / Potential Cross-Site Scripting
description: Static analysis identified HTML-generation patterns where dynamic values may reach HTML rendering contexts. The issue is exploitable only if attacker-controlled data can reach an executable HTML/JavaScript sink without appropriate encoding or sanitization.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Identify the current static-analysis finding.
2. Determine whether the value originates from an untrusted source.
3. Trace it to the HTML sink.
4. Use a harmless local XSS test marker.
5. Determine whether it is rendered as HTML or text.
proof_of_concept: Safe Proof of Concept: Use only an isolated local test value such as . Do not use credential theft, cookie extraction, data exfiltration, or persistent payloads.
business_impact: A confirmed XSS issue could allow attacker-controlled JavaScript to execute in a victim's browser context.
remediation: Prefer React's escaped rendering, avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML unless necessary, sanitize required HTML, apply context-specific output encoding, and use CSP as defense in depth.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Eliminate dangerouslySetInnerHTML usages where standard React JSX string interpolation can be used.
2. When rich HTML rendering is essential, sanitize markup using DOMPurify with strict attribute allowlists.
3. Enforce a restrictive Content Security Policy that bans inline scripts.

title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Candidate
description: Static analysis identified dynamic URL/request handling that may potentially allow user-controlled URLs to be requested by the server. Exploitability requires confirmation that an untrusted input reaches a server-side request sink.
affected_component: src/App.ts / map components / server-side request handling
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Identify the server-side request function.
2. Trace its URL source.
3. Determine whether the URL is user-controlled.
4. Use a local HTTP test server.
5. Confirm whether the application's server makes the request.
proof_of_concept:
Safe Proof of Concept:
Use only a local endpoint such as http://127.0.0.1:8000/test that you control. Do not probe cloud metadata endpoints, internal networks, or third-party systems.
business_impact: If confirmed, SSRF could allow requests from the application's network environment to resources inaccessible directly from the Internet.
remediation: Allowlist destinations and schemes, validate hostnames/IPs, block private/internal ranges where appropriate, restrict outbound network access, and avoid arbitrary client-supplied URLs.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Enforce strict destination allowlisting for external API endpoints.
2. Validate resolved IP addresses to block RFC1918 private ranges and cloud metadata services (169.254.169.254).
3. Disable HTTP redirection following in server-side HTTP client instances.

title: Potential Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS)
description: Static analysis identified dynamically constructed regular expressions. The risk depends on whether untrusted input can influence the pattern and whether the resulting expression has excessive computational complexity.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Identify the dynamic regex construction.
2. Determine whether an attacker can influence the pattern.
3. Test only with bounded input in a local environment.
4. Measure execution time.
5. Determine whether processing grows disproportionately.
proof_of_concept:
Safe Proof of Concept:
Use small, bounded local test strings and measure execution time. Do not send high-volume requests or intentionally overload a live system.
business_impact: A confirmed ReDoS condition could consume excessive CPU and degrade application availability.
remediation: Prefer fixed regex patterns, avoid constructing regexes from untrusted input, limit input length, and use safe regex patterns.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Replace dynamic regex construction with static, pre-compiled regular expressions.
2. Audit expressions for nested quantifiers and overlapping subpatterns (catastrophic backtracking).
3. Use linear-time regular expression engines (such as re2) where user-supplied queries are permitted.

title: Unsafe Dynamic Script Generation / Potential XSS
description: Static analysis identified dynamically generated script/HTML content involving values such as bundle and pageUrl. This becomes a vulnerability if attacker-controlled data reaches an executable script context.
parameter: bundle and pageUrl dynamic script concatenation
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Identify the dynamically inserted value.
2. Trace its source.
3. Determine whether it can be attacker-controlled.
4. Run script generation locally.
5. Inspect the generated HTML/script.
proof_of_concept:
Safe Proof of Concept:
Use a harmless local marker such as XSS-TEST and inspect whether it is inserted into an executable context without safe serialization or encoding.
business_impact: If attacker-controlled data reaches executable script context, malicious JavaScript could potentially execute in users' browsers.
remediation: Avoid concatenating untrusted input into JavaScript, use safe serialization, validate generated URLs, avoid dynamic script generation where possible, and use CSP as defense in depth.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Use JSON.stringify() or safe serialization functions rather than raw string interpolation for inline variables.
2. Validate that pageUrl matches approved protocols (https:) and domain allowlists.
3. Prefer static bundling workflows over runtime dynamic script emission.

title: Supply-Chain Configuration Weakness — Dependabot Cooldown
description: Static analysis identified a dependency-management configuration weakness: the expected Dependabot cooldown configuration is absent. This is a security configuration finding rather than a direct exploit by itself.
steps_to_reproduce:
1. Open .github/dependabot.yml.
2. Review dependency update configuration.
3. Confirm the expected cooldown setting is absent.
4. Review the dependency update workflow and approval process.
proof_of_concept:
Safe Proof of Concept:
No exploit is required. The PoC is configuration evidence showing the dependency update policy and absence of the expected cooldown control.
business_impact: Rapid dependency updates can increase supply-chain risk if a newly published package version is compromised or introduces an unexpected security issue.
remediation: Configure an appropriate dependency update cooldown and review policy. Maintain dependency review, lockfiles, vulnerability monitoring, automated testing, and controlled update procedures.
remediation_recommendations:
1. Establish a minimum cooldown delay (e.g., 3-7 days) for non-critical dependency updates to allow public malicious package detection.
2. Mandate branch protection, CI automated test passes, and manual peer review on all automated pull requests.
3. Lock dependency versions using package-lock.json and integrate automated vulnerability scanning (npm audit / Snyk).
